title: A hymn in Gond
hookLine: Gond holds Kabir's song of the elephant that would not charge, and the judge who still didn't see

lines: A JUDGE, A DRIVER, AN ELEPHANT.
cards: Three look at the same thing and see three different things. A judge sees a troublemaker who has to be made an example of. A driver sees an order he can't refuse, and a threat against his own life.
And an elephant, huge and goaded, looks down at a man tied up in a bundle and sees something neither of the others can. You met this hymn of Kabir's earlier on the path. This time, watch the eyes.

teach.h: THE STRENGTH IS YOURS, MY LORD.
teach.b: First, the refrain, the line the whole hymn turns on, on ang eight seventy. In paraphrase: O my Lord, the strength is yours. Kabir doesn't say the elephant was gentle, or that he was clever.
He sets the whole story under that line. Second, the driver. The judge, the qazi, shouts at him: drive it on, or I'll cut you to pieces; goad it, beat it.
The driver strikes the elephant on the head.
He sees an order and a threat, and obeys. The hymn doesn't curse him. It shows a man too frightened to see anything else.

teach.h: THE ELEPHANT SEES THE LORD, AND BOWS.
teach.b: Third, the elephant. It runs off crying out, and Kabir hears it say: I am a sacrifice to this form.
Then it stands still, in meditation, because the Lord dwells in its heart. It lifts the bundle again and again, and bows. Fourth, the judge.
Kabir asks him plainly: what wrong has this saint done, that you tied him up and gave him to the elephant? The verdict is about eyes: the qazi, in his darkness, didn't understand.
Three times, the hymn says, he put it to the test, and his hard heart still wasn't convinced. Seeing isn't only about what's in front of you. It's about the heart doing the looking.
The judge looked straight at a wonder and saw nothing, while the beast he meant as a weapon saw the Lord.

how: Kabir's Gond hymn of the elephant is sung in kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers retell it as a story of the devotee protected by the Lord, whose strength the refrain names.

games.q: what does “a hymn in gond” mean?
o: Kabir's song of an elephant that bowed instead of charging
a hymn about an elephant a king gave to the Guru
a story of a driver who refused the judge's orders

games.q: who sees what in Kabir's hymn — tap the pairs.
p: O my Lord, the strength is yours

s: the hymn curses the elephant driver
it shows him frightened and obeying, and doesn't curse him.
the judge is convinced once he sees the elephant bow
three times, the hymn says, he put it to the test, and his hard heart still wasn't convinced.
Kabir credits the Lord's strength, not his own
the refrain: O my Lord, the strength is yours.

games.q: you're the elephant. the goad strikes your head, the judge is shouting, and a bound man lies in front of you. what do you do?
o: charge, as you've been driven to.
run off, then stand still and bow to the bundle.
throw the driver and leave the yard.
games.why: the elephant runs off crying out, then stands still in meditation, lifts the bundle again and again, and bows, because the Lord dwells in its heart.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've already made up your mind about, someone you see as a problem, though not someone who has harmed you, and hold their face.

Then slowly look at them the way the elephant looked at the bundle on the ground: not as a target or an order, but as someone the Lord might live inside; you don't have to change your mind, just look once more, with one Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Gond. Kabir's song of the elephant that would not charge: a frightened driver, a judge who didn't see, and a refrain that says the strength is yours. Today's word.

orig.note: kunchar, elephant, the word Kabir's hymn uses when the elephant lifts the bundle and bows.

carryVoice: Your line: the elephant bowed. A second look can see what the first one missed. Another week, done.
